title: How to Set Multi-Currency Prices and Rounding Rules Without Losing Margin
excerpt: Auto converted prices look careless and leak margin. This guide covers setting price points per market, rounding rules that round in your favour, and a reprice trigger tied to a currency band rather than a calendar.
body: Turning on automatic currency conversion takes five minutes and quietly damages two things. The first is trust: a product priced at forty dollars becomes an odd figure in pounds that reads like a number nobody chose. The second is margin, because the display conversion and the settlement rate differ, with fees between them. The fix is manual price points per market plus a rounding rule, and a trigger that tells you when a price has drifted far enough to be worth changing.

Set one price per currency per product, and choose it as a price point instead of a conversion. Buyers compare against local competitors, so an ending that looks conventional in that market matters more than mathematical accuracy. Nine endings work in some markets and round numbers in others, and the wrong ending signals a foreign store. Write the ending down once per currency and apply it everywhere so the catalog looks deliberate. Also keep a floor price per product per currency, built from landed cost, fees and target margin, because that floor stops a discount from becoming a loss.

Rounding needs one direction, and it is up. When you convert an internal target price into a local currency, always round to the next valid price point rather than to the nearest, and never round down for a nicer number. Then define the band: the currency movement you absorb before repricing. Three to five percent works for most catalogs. Inside the band you do nothing, because frequent changes confuse returning buyers and create conversations about the same product costing less last week. Outside the band you reprice the affected currency in one scheduled pass.

Run reprice passes on a fixed schedule rather than whenever a rate moves. Pull the current rate, apply your spread assumption including processor and payout fees, recompute the local price, round up to the next valid point, then compare against the floor. Anything that would land below the floor does not get discounted to stay attractive; it gets paused in that market or published at the floor with the margin noted. Keep a table with rate, fee assumption, computed price, published price and floor, because that is what you need when someone asks why a price rose.

Two rules keep this from becoming a treadmill. Do not reprice one product because a competitor moved; reprice the currency or leave it alone. Do not change prices during a live promotion, since the comparison a buyer makes is against the price they saw yesterday, not against your costs. Expect a short conversion dip after a rise and measure it over two weeks before reversing anything. A market with constant currency movement deserves a wider band rather than more frequent passes, because repricing spends a little trust each time.

Check the settlement side once a quarter. Payout timing, the rate applied at settlement and the fee deducted are three separate numbers, and the gap between the displayed price and what actually arrives is the only margin figure that matters. Reconcile a sample of orders against the price table you maintain and adjust the spread assumption when it is wrong. The DTCwise Payments & FX category at /category/payments keeps the current shortlist with ratings and pricing, and /tool/airwallex covers the settlement detail behind the rules.
